## Motivation

Why convert text to numbers?

- Neural networks operate on numbers  
- Text is symbolic  
- We must encode text numerically  

Pipeline:

$$
\text{Text} \rightarrow \text{Tokens} \rightarrow \text{IDs} \rightarrow
\text{Embeddings} \rightarrow \text{Tensors}
$$

---

## Predictive Modeling Analogy

Classical ML:

$$
(X_1, X_2, \dots, X_k) \rightarrow y
$$

Text modeling:

$$
(t_{i-2},\, t_{i-1}) \rightarrow t_i
$$

Next-token prediction = supervised learning on sequences.

---

## Tokenization

Tokenization breaks text into:

- Word tokens  
- Subword tokens (BPE)  
- Characters  

Models do **not** understand words.  
Models understand **token IDs**.

---

## Example Sentence

Sentence:

I love large language models.


Tokens:

I
love
large
language
models
.


---

## Vocabulary → Token IDs

Mapping:

$$
\begin{array}{c|c}
\text{Token} & \text{ID} \\
\hline
\text{I} & 1 \\
\text{love} & 2 \\
\text{large} & 3 \\
\text{language} & 4 \\
\text{models} & 5 \\
\text{.} & 6
\end{array}
$$

Encoded sentence:

$$[1,2,3,4,5,6]$$

---

## Context Window

Assume:

- context length = 2  
- predict the next token  

Training examples:

$$
[I,\, love] \rightarrow large
$$

$$
[love,\, large] \rightarrow language
$$

$$
[large,\, language] \rightarrow models
$$

$$
[language,\, models] \rightarrow .
$$

---

## Embedding Layer

Token IDs → dense vectors  
Embedding dimension = **3**

Example embeddings:

$$
\begin{array}{c|c}
\text{Token} & \text{Embedding} \\
\hline
\text{I} & (0.1,\;0.2,\;0.3) \\
\text{love} & (-0.5,\;0.1,\;0.0) \\
\text{large} & (0.7,\;-0.2,\;0.4) \\
\text{language} & (0.0,\;0.3,\;0.9) \\
\text{models} & (0.4,\;0.4,\;0.4) \\
\text{.} & (-0.2,\;0.0,\;0.1)
\end{array}
$$

---

## Converting Tokens to Embeddings

Example input:


Tensor (shape 2 × 3):

$$
\begin{pmatrix}
0.1 & 0.2 & 0.3 \\
-0.5 & 0.1 & 0.0
\end{pmatrix}
$$

---

## Full Training Examples

Context length = 2, embed dim = 3:

$$
[1,2] \rightarrow
\begin{pmatrix}
0.1 & 0.2 & 0.3 \\
-0.5 & 0.1 & 0.0
\end{pmatrix}
$$

$$
[2,3] \rightarrow
\begin{pmatrix}
-0.5 & 0.1 & 0.0 \\
0.7 & -0.2 & 0.4
\end{pmatrix}
$$

$$
[3,4] \rightarrow
\begin{pmatrix}
0.7 & -0.2 & 0.4 \\
0.0 & 0.3 & 0.9
\end{pmatrix}
$$

$$
[4,5] \rightarrow
\begin{pmatrix}
0.0 & 0.3 & 0.9 \\
0.4 & 0.4 & 0.4
\end{pmatrix}
$$

Targets:

$$[3,\;4,\;5,\;6]$$

---

## Next Token Prediction

The model learns:

$$
f: \mathbb{R}^{2 \times 3} \rightarrow \text{Probabilities over tokens}
$$

Example distribution:

- P(large) = 0.72  
- P(language) = 0.10  
- P(models) = 0.08  
- P(.) = 0.02  

Prediction = highest probability.

---

## Regression Analogy

| Text Modeling Concept | Regression Equivalent |
|-----------------------|-----------------------|
| Previous tokens | Input \(X\) |
| Next token | Output \(y\) |
| Token IDs | Encoded categorical vars |
| Embeddings | Learned numeric features |
| Context window | # predictors |
| Sequence model | \(f(X)\) |

---

## Before Transformers

RNN/LSTM:

- Reads text sequentially  
- Memory fades  
- Struggles with long-range relationships  

Transformers solve these.

---

## Transformers (High-Level Summary)

Transformers add:

- Positional encoding  
- Multi-head self-attention  
- Feed-forward layers  
- Parallelism  

But the input is still the **same embedding tensor**.

---

## Key Takeaways

- Text → tokens → IDs → embeddings → tensors  
- NLP is supervised learning on sequences  
- Embeddings are learned numeric features  
- Context window = model's view  
- LLMs predict **one token at a time**
